title: IB Predicted Grades vs Final Grades Explained
summary: Learn how IB predicted grades are set, why final results differ, how grade boundaries affect outcomes, and what students and parents should do next.
body_markdown:
**IB predicted grades vs final grades** are related, but they are not calculated in the same way. A predicted grade is a teacher's evidence-based forecast of likely achievement. A final grade is the official result produced from assessed work, component weightings, moderation, marking, and session-specific grade boundaries.


Predictions can influence university applications, especially conditional offers, but they are not guarantees. Subject predictions often match or come within one grade of the final result, while exact Diploma totals are harder to predict because differences across six subjects and the core can accumulate.


### IB predicted grades vs final grades at a glance


Feature Predicted grade Final grade


Who determines it? Subject teacher and school The IB through its assessment process


When is it set? Before final results, often during DP2 After assessed components are completed and marked


Main evidence Mocks, tests, coursework, class performance, and IB standards Examinations, internally assessed work, externally assessed coursework, TOK, and the Extended Essay


Subject scale 1-7 1-7


Main purpose Forecast achievement and support applications Record official achievement and determine Diploma outcomes


Part of the final calculation? Normally no It is the official outcome


The IB defines a **predicted grade** as the grade a teacher expects a candidate to achieve based on available evidence and knowledge of IB standards. Predictions are also submitted for **Theory of Knowledge** and the **Extended Essay** using their respective scales.


### How IB predicted grades are set


There is no worldwide formula requiring every school to weight evidence identically. Teachers are expected to make the most accurate professional judgment possible rather than deliberately overpredicting or underpredicting.


Evidence may include:


- Timed mock examinations and topic tests
- Internal Assessment progress or completed work
- Essays, oral tasks, practical work, performances, or portfolios
- Consistency and sustainable improvement across DP1 and DP2
- Official assessment criteria and grade descriptors
- Historical boundaries used cautiously as guides


A prediction should represent the grade a student is **expected to achieve** , not the highest possible result under ideal conditions. Effort and potential provide context, but they should not replace evidence demonstrating the relevant standard.


Schools may create university application predictions before submitting official predictions to the IB. Because these may use different deadlines and evidence, students should ask which prediction is being discussed and whether reconsideration is possible. See RevisionDojo's guides to[predicted grades and university offers](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/predicted-grades-and-university-offers) and[maximizing predicted and final grades](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/final-ib-year-maximize-predicted-final-grades) .


### How final IB grades are calculated


A final subject grade follows the assessment model in the current subject guide. Depending on the course, this may include examination papers, an Internal Assessment, oral work, portfolios, performances, or externally assessed coursework.


The process generally involves:


1. Marking each assessment component.
2. Moderating internally assessed work where applicable.
3. Scaling component marks according to official weightings.
4. Combining the weighted marks into an overall subject mark.
5. Comparing that mark with the session's **grade boundaries** .
6. Awarding a final subject grade from **1-7** .


The IB's[assessment guide for students and parents](https://www.ibo.org/contentassets/8ecbee9f96af4db98293b97c133516f5/students-and-parents-amended.pdf) distinguishes marks from grades. Marks show how much credit work earned, while grades describe the standard demonstrated. Consequently, the same percentage does not automatically produce the same grade across subjects or sessions.


### How grade boundaries affect results


**IB grade boundaries** are cut-off marks used to convert aggregated marks into grades. They are established using examiner judgment, candidate work, grade descriptors, statistical evidence, and feedback about the examinations.


Boundaries can change when paper difficulty changes. A demanding paper may have a lower boundary, while an easier paper may have a higher one. Historical boundaries are useful estimates, but they cannot reveal future cut-offs and must match the correct subject, level, syllabus, and session.


RevisionDojo explains[how IB grade boundaries work](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-grade-boundaries-explained) . Its[IB Grade Calculator](https://www.revisiondojo.com/grade-calculator) can convert representative practice marks into an estimate, but this is not an official result or guarantee.


### How often predictions and final grades differ


The IB does not publish one worldwide prediction-accuracy rate covering every school and session. However, an independent analysis of **143,874 subject predictions** from 70 schools found that approximately **50%** matched the awarded grade, **27%** were higher, and **23%** were lower. The average absolute difference was about **0.5 subject-grade points** .


Exact Diploma totals were less common. About **15%** matched exactly, while approximately **66%** were within 2 points and **81%** were within 3 points. This is unsurprising because several small subject differences can accumulate across the Diploma score.


These are not official global IB statistics. School calibration, subjects, cohorts, and assessment conditions affect accuracy, and underprediction can occur as well as overprediction. The most defensible conclusion is that subject predictions are often close, while exact totals out of 45 are substantially harder to forecast. RevisionDojo provides further analysis of[predicted versus final-grade accuracy](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-predicted-vs-final-grades-how-accurate-are-they-and-what-history-shows) .


### Why final grades may differ


Common reasons include:


- **Examination performance:** Revision may produce improvement, while anxiety, timing problems, illness, or incomplete answers may reduce marks.
- **IA moderation:** The IB can adjust internally awarded marks when a sampled department's marking is too generous or severe.
- **Different weightings:** School predictions may emphasize mocks, while final results follow the subject's official component weightings.
- **Boundary movement:** Teachers predict before final boundaries are known, so candidates near a cut-off may move either way.
- **Cumulative differences:** Two subjects finishing one grade lower can turn a predicted 38 into a final 36 without a dramatic overall collapse.


### What students should do


Treat a prediction as a planning estimate rather than a result already earned. Record each subject's components, weightings, target grade, current evidence, and recurring weaknesses. Then complete timed practice, classify lost marks, repair specific gaps, attempt unfamiliar questions, and retest independently.


Track several performances rather than relying on one unusually strong mock. RevisionDojo's[Mock Exams guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/revisiondojo-mock-exams) , Questionbank, Study Notes, Flashcards, and Jojo AI can support this process, although final checks should be completed without hints.


If final grades are lower than predicted, compare them with the university's precise conditions. Offers may specify an overall total, Higher Level grades, or named subjects. Ask the coordinator for available marks and boundary information, as explained in the[IB assessment FAQ](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/assessment-and-exams/getting-results/assessment-faq/) .


An **Enquiry Upon Results** may be appropriate when a result appears inconsistent with the assessed standard. It is not a request for extra marks merely because a candidate is close to a boundary, and marks can move in either direction. Students should also contact the university promptly because it may confirm the place, offer an alternative, or wait for a review.


### Common misconceptions


- **A predicted 7 guarantees a final 7.** It is an evidence-based expectation, not a promise.
- **The IB copies predicted grades.** Normal final grades come from assessed components and boundaries.
- **Boundaries are fixed percentages.** They can vary between subjects and sessions.
- **A lower result proves the prediction was poor.** Examinations, moderation, weighting, and boundaries may contribute.


### Conclusion


In **IB predicted grades vs final grades** , the prediction is a professional forecast, while the final grade is the official assessment outcome. Students should focus on producing consistent evidence under realistic conditions rather than treating a prediction as secured.
